title: A memory problem
question: The last character hides the difference.
explanation: Part One could finish cat, car, and can. Now we extend its training examples into three sentences. When the prompt ends in “is ”, the last character is a space in every case. Our tiny model looks up the same row and makes the same prediction, even though the earlier subject differs.
caption: This is a new training collection, not knowledge contained in the original ten words. We still use character tokens. The experiment below counts real transitions from these three sentences.
next: First, try giving the count model more memory.

title: Remember more
question: Look up several previous characters instead of one.
explanation: Instead of a row for “ ”, use a row for the last three characters, “is ”. That is still the same for all three prompts. Eight characters retain the subject and can distinguish “ cat is ”, “ car is ”, and “ can is ”. Move the context control below and watch which earlier characters remain visible.
caption: More context solves this distinction in the training collection. It does not automatically solve unfamiliar text.
next: A longer lookup has a catch: what if that exact context never appeared?

title: Missing combinations
question: An exact lookup can have no answer.
explanation: Choose “the cab is ” in the experiment. Its eight-character context was never observed, so there is no row to look up. A shorter context can provide a fallback, and adding small counts can avoid zero probabilities. Those are useful count-model improvements—but neither creates an understanding of the new subject.
caption: An unseen row is different from a low-probability outcome in an existing row. Neural models can also fail on unfamiliar inputs; they do not create missing knowledge for free.
next: Can we reuse pieces of what we learned, rather than demand a separate row for every full context?

title: Share a calculation
question: Separate rows cannot share what they learn.
explanation: Longer contexts create many possible combinations. A counting table stores the observed combinations separately. A neural model instead uses a shared calculation whose adjustable numbers are reused for many inputs. This can help generalization; it is a different approach, not a requirement for our original tiny task.

example.label: Count approach
example.value: exact context → its own count row

caption: With V tokens there are Vᵏ possible contexts of length k. A sparse table stores only observed ones, but then many combinations remain missing.
next: A shared calculation needs an input representation with adjustable values, rather than just an arbitrary token label.

title: Vectors & embeddings
question: Store a small recipe for each token.
explanation: Give every character an ID to locate it in a table. Its row contains several adjustable numbers: a vector. When that row represents a token, it is called an embedding. The entries tell later calculations how strongly to use different shared patterns. The ID finds the row; the embedding supplies values to calculate with.

example.label: Meaning in our toy calculation
example.value: amount of pattern A; amount of pattern B

caption: A and B below are deliberately simple scoring patterns. In a real model their meanings are not hand-assigned; embeddings and shared calculations learn together. These entries are not probabilities.
next: Let’s make the recipe do something visible, using the same t/r/n choices from Part One.

title: From recipe to scores
question: A weight multiplies a contribution.
explanation: A weight is an adjustable multiplier: 2 doubles a number, 0 removes its contribution, and a negative value reverses its sign. Use the embedding [0.75, 0.25] to multiply two shared patterns, then add. This gives a score for each possible next character. Higher scores express stronger preference, not percentages.

example.label: Shared pattern A, for [t, r, n]
Shared pattern B, for [t, r, n]

caption: This is a toy output calculation, not a trained sentence model. A full model scores every token in its vocabulary. Grouping these multiply-and-add calculations into a table is matrix multiplication.
next: These predictions only become useful when the recipe and patterns are adjusted using real examples.

title: Learn the numbers
question: Replace invented settings with practice.
explanation: Softmax converts scores into probabilities. Loss measures how little probability the model assigned to the observed next token. Gradients tell us how a small change to each adjustable number would affect that loss; backpropagation computes them through the calculation. An optimizer then takes a small update step. Repeat this across examples to train the embeddings and weights together.
caption: The numbers above illustrate the starting mismatch; this page does not run neural training. Softmax uses exponentials and normalization. Repeated examples guide the probabilities; no single update is guaranteed to improve every example.
next: Token embeddings can now be useful inputs. For longer text, we still need to preserve order and combine context.

title: Preserve order
question: A bag of token vectors loses the sentence.
explanation: The words cat and act contain the same characters. Looking up their embeddings gives the same three rows in different orders. If we simply add the rows, the result is identical. Position information lets later calculations distinguish where each token occurred.

example.label: cat
example.value: c at 1 · a at 2 · t at 3

example.label: act
example.value: a at 1 · c at 2 · t at 3

caption: There are several ways to supply position information. The purpose is to distinguish order; it does not by itself decide which information matters.
next: Now the model can combine information from different positions without treating every position identically.

title: Use relevant context
question: Calculate a different mixture for each context.
explanation: Attention compares the current representation with available positions and turns comparison scores into mixing shares. It combines their information using those shares. Unlike a fixed lookup row, this mixture depends on the input. To complete “the cat is ”, the model can use information from the earlier subject as well as the final space.
caption: The diagram uses invented shares and simplified vectors, not learned explanations for the sentence. Future positions must be masked during training so the model cannot read the answer ahead. Attention alone is not a complete transformer.
next: The context-dependent result feeds later transformations and the output-score calculation.

title: Put the pieces together
question: Attention needs a surrounding prediction model.
explanation: A small decoder-only transformer combines token representations and position information with causal attention and a feedforward network. The feedforward network applies learned transformations and a nonlinear rule, allowing more than one linear remix. Residual connections carry an earlier representation forward; normalization helps control numerical scales. These blocks produce a vector used to score next tokens.
caption: This is the assembly map, not a full implementation tutorial. Residual connections and normalization belong around the block operations. Every added component must be trained; adding it does not automatically improve quality.
next: Once trained, generation is still the same loop you already understand.

title: The same generation loop
question: Only the prediction machinery has changed.
explanation: Part One looked up a count row. The neural version calculates probabilities from a learned representation of the context. Both choose a token, append it, and repeat until END or a length limit. During generation, the learned weights stay fixed. Evaluate on held-out text to check whether the extra machinery actually helped.
caption: The neural model can still generate incorrect or meaningless text. More context and shared representations offer capacity; sufficient data, training, and evaluation determine whether that capacity is useful.
next: Return to the tiny model whenever you want to see the complete generation loop without the extra machinery.
